newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Antonov to sell first An-38 jets in '97.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Antonov to sell first An-38 jets in '97.

text.p: Ukraine's Antonov design bureau and plane-maker will start selling its new An-38 small passenger jet this year, a spokesman said on Monday.
Vitaly Kulakov, Antonov's Deputy Marketing Director, also said tests on the new An-70 military and cargo plane were going well and 20 flights had been carried out.
"Already at least three An-38 planes have been ordered by Russian companies and will be delivered by the end of the year.
"We have orders for two years. Dozens of planes were ordered by contract and up to 200 planes will be sold if the intentions of carriers become reality," he said.

The An-38 can carry 27 passengers or up to 2.5 tonnes of cargo for 900 km (550 miles) without refuelling. It will cost $4.2-4.5 million, less than western-made equivalents and the Czech-made L-410 jet.
Antonov said in a statement that three other models would be produced in addition to the passenger one -- business, medical and patrol jets.
Kulakov said the An-38, aimed at replacing the An-28, was being produced at a plant in the Russian city of Novosibirsk by the Ukrainian-Russian venture "Sibirskiye Samolyoty Antonov".
Antonov said the new jet was aimed at markets in Russia and other post-Soviet states as well as Latin America, South-East Asia and the Middle East.
"This plane is quite good for countries with hot climates and for mountainous areas. It can land and take off at heights of 4,000 metres, (13,000 feet) " Kulakov said.
"World estimates say 2,600 planes of such a class will be needed in the next 15 years," Kulakov said.
"We would be happy to get a quarter or a third of the potential orders."
An-38 has engines made by U.S. Allied-Signal and props from another American company, Hartzell.
Kulakov also said the first model of a new short-haul turboprop An-140 aimed at replacing thousands of An-24s widely used in former Soviet and developing countries had been built.
The An-140 would cost $6.5 million -- half the price of Western-made equivalents, the ATR-42, Fokker-50 and Dash-8, Antonov said in a press release.
The first An-140 model will start test flights either in August or September, Kulakov said, adding that Antonov aimed to get an international certificate for it by the end of 1998.
An-140 can carry 52 passengers or 4.9 tonnes of cargo for 2,100 kilometres (1,100 miles).
Kulakov said the new An-70 cargo plane which had made 20 successful flights would go into mass production next year.
Designed for civilian and military purposes, it can carry 35 tonnes of cargo for 3,500 km (2,200 miles).
